## Introduction

In the context of sports analytics, predictive modeling is used for
evaluating player performance and categorizing athletes into meaningful
tiers based on their on-court contributions. This study focuses on the
classification of basketball players into three performance levels —
Low, Average, and Elite — based on a set of performance-related metrics
such as usage percentage (USG%), true shooting percentage (TS%), net
rating, and other physical and statistical indicators. To achieve this,
we constructed a multi-class target variable pts_level from players'
average points per game (PTS) using domain-informed thresholds. We then
applied a suite of supervised machine learning models to predict
pts_level, including a simple baseline multinomial logistic regression
model (using nnet), an elastic net-regularized multinomial logistic
regression (via glmnet), a random forest classifier, and a support
vector machine (SVM) with a radial basis function kernel. One model was
designed with a focus on interpretability, while another prioritized
predictive accuracy. In addition, we implemented a custom multinomial
logistic regression model trained using our own gradient descent
algorithm. This was done to demonstrate a deeper understanding of
optimization methods beyond standard packages. All models were trained
using 5-fold cross-validation and evaluated on a held-out test set.
Metrics such as classification accuracy, ROC AUC, sensitivity, and
specificity were used for performance comparison. This comparative
modeling approach allows us to identify tradeoffs between
interpretability and predictive power in multi-class classification,
with practical implications for player evaluation and decision support
in sports analytics.

The central motivating question of this project is: Can we use
statistical and machine learning methods to meaningfully classify NBA
players into scoring tiers based on their performance metrics, and
balance the tradeoff between interpretability and predictive accuracy?

## Data Cleaning

The original dataset was cleaned and preprocessed to ensure data
consistency and readiness for modeling. The following steps were
applied: "None" values in the college column were replaced with
"Unknown" and converted to a factor. The draft_year, draft_round, and
draft_number columns were cleaned by replacing empty strings and
"Undrafted" with a unified "Undrafted" label, then converted to
categorical factors. Missing values in five key numeric features
(oreb_pct, dreb_pct, usg_pct, ts_pct, and ast_pct) were imputed using
median values. Outliers in the net_rating column were removed by
filtering to the range [-100, 100]. Players with fewer than 5 games
played (gp \< 5) were excluded from the analysis to reduce noise.
Although the season variable was already in the correct format
(YYYY-YY), a cleaning pipeline was applied to ensure consistent
formatting; this had no functional effect in this dataset. After
cleaning, the dataset was ready for downstream exploratory analysis and
predictive modeling.

```{r}
# Load and clean NBA player season data
# Load the data
data <- read.csv("data/all_seasons.csv") 

# Replace "None" in the college column with "Unknown" and convert to a factor
data$college <- factor(ifelse(data$college == "None", "Unknown", data$college))

# Uniformly set "Undrafted" or empty strings "" in the draft_year, draft_round, and draft_number columns to "Undrafted" and convert to factors
for (col in c('draft_year', 'draft_round', 'draft_number')) {
  data[[col]] <- factor(ifelse(data[[col]] %in% c("Undrafted", ""), "Undrafted", data[[col]]))
}

# Fill missing values in the oreb_pct, dreb_pct, usg_pct, ts_pct, and ast_pct columns with medians
for (col in c('oreb_pct', 'dreb_pct', 'usg_pct', 'ts_pct', 'ast_pct')) {
  median_value <- median(data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  data[[col]] <- ifelse(is.na(data[[col]]), median_value, data[[col]])
}

# Remove extreme values outside the [-100, 100] range in the net_rating column
data <- data[data$net_rating >= -100 & data$net_rating <= 100, ]

# Keep only data of players with games played (gp) of at least 5
data <- data[data$gp >= 5, ]


# Clean and standardize the season data
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    season_clean = case_when(
      grepl("^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}$", season) ~ season,  # Original standard format
      TRUE ~ {
        # First convert to a real date (e.g., Jan-00 → 2000-01-01)
        real_date <- suppressWarnings(dmy(paste0("01-", season)))
        year_val <- year(real_date)
        month_val <- month(real_date)

        # If it is the first half of the year (January–June), the season starts from the previous year
        season_start <- ifelse(month_val <= 6, year_val - 1, year_val)
        paste0(season_start, "-", sprintf("%02d", (season_start + 1) %% 100))
      }
    )
  )


data <- data %>%
  select(-season) %>%
  rename(season = season_clean)

data <- subset(data, select = -X)

```

## Data Preprocessing

In this step, we performed several key preprocessing tasks to prepare
the data for modeling. A new categorical variable, pts_level, was
generated based on players' points per game (pts). Players were
classified into 3 performance levels: "Low" (less than 10 points),
"Average" (between 10 and 20 points) and "Elite" (20 points or more).
This variable was then converted into a factor with a specified level
order ("Low", "Average", "Elite"). The dataset was randomly split into a
training set and a test set using an 80/20 split.

```{r}
set.seed(123)  

# Create categorical scoring levels and split into train/test sets
# Recreate pts_level as a factor with specified level order (optional)
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    pts_level = case_when(
      pts >= 20 ~ "Elite",
      pts >= 10 & pts < 20 ~ "Average",
      TRUE ~ "Low"
    ),
    pts_level = factor(pts_level, levels = c("Low", "Average", "Elite")) 
  )

# Split data into training and test sets
data_split <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.8) 
train_data <- training(data_split) 
test_data <- testing(data_split) 
```

## Data Dictionary

**Variable** \| **Description**

`player_name` \| Name of the basketball player.\
`team_abbreviation` \| Abbreviated team name the player belongs to.\
`age` \| Player’s age (in years).\
`player_height` \| Player’s height (in centimeters).\
`player_weight` \| Player’s weight (in kilograms).\
`college` \| College or university the player attended (if any),
otherwise marked as "Unknown".\
`country` \| Country of origin or nationality of the player.\
`draft_year` \| Year the player was drafted to the NBA; "Undrafted" if
not selected.\
`draft_round` \| Draft round when the player was selected; "Undrafted"
if not selected.\
`draft_number` \| Overall draft pick number; "Undrafted" if not
selected.\
`gp` \| Games played in the season.\
`pts` \| Average points scored per game.\
`reb` \| Average rebounds per game.\
`ast` \| Average assists per game.\
`net_rating` \| Net rating (points scored minus points allowed per 100
possessions when the player is on the court).\
`oreb_pct` \| Offensive rebound percentage: share of available offensive
rebounds collected by the player.\
`dreb_pct` \| Defensive rebound percentage: share of available defensive
rebounds collected by the player.\
`usg_pct` \| Usage percentage: share of team plays used by the player
while on the court.\
`ts_pct` \| True shooting percentage: efficiency metric that accounts
for field goals, three-pointers, and free throws.\
`ast_pct` \| Assist percentage: estimate of teammates' field goals
assisted while the player is on the court.\
`pts_level` \| Categorical target variable based on average points per
game: Low (\<10), Average (10–19), Elite (≥20).

`season` \| Basketball season, formatted as "YYYY-YY" (e.g., 2019–20).

## Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

### Descriptive Statistics

To gain an initial understanding of the dataset, we conducted both
numerical and categorical summaries. Numerical variables were summarized
using standard descriptive statistics, including mean, standard
deviation, quartiles and range. Categorical variables (such as
team_abbreviation, country, draft_roundand the derived target variable
pts_level) were summarized using frequency counts and proportions.

Additionally, we visualized the distributions of key numeric features
using raincloud plots, which combine density curves, boxplots, and
jittered points to highlight spread and skewness. Finally, we plotted a
pie chart to display the class distribution of the target variable
pts_level.

The class distribution reveals a clear imbalance, approximately 67% of
players are classified as Elite, 27% as Low, and only 6% as Average.
This imbalance suggests that models need to be evaluated carefully,
especially on metrics sensitive to minority class performance such as
sensitivity, specificity and F1-score, to ensure they are not simply
overfitting to the dominant Elite class.

```{r}
# Summarize numerical and categorical variables
# Descriptive statistics for numerical variables
numeric_stats <- data %>%
  select(where(is.numeric) & !starts_with("X")) %>%  
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") %>%  
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Define categorical variables
categorical_vars <- c("team_abbreviation", "country", "draft_round", "pts_level")

# Define a helper function to process each categorical variable
process_categorical_var <- function(var_name) {
  var_data <- data[[var_name]]
  
  # Handle missing values
  if(any(is.na(var_data))) {
    var_data <- var_data[!is.na(var_data)]
  }
  
  # Use table() function to count frequencies
  freq_table <- table(var_data)
  
  # Convert to data frame
  result_df <- data.frame(
    variable = var_name,
    category = names(freq_table),
    count = as.numeric(freq_table),
    proportion = as.numeric(freq_table) / sum(freq_table)
  )
  
  return(result_df)
}

# Apply the function to all categorical variables
categorical_stats <- map_dfr(categorical_vars, process_categorical_var)


# Print results
print(numeric_stats, n = Inf)
categorical_stats <- as_tibble(categorical_stats)
print(categorical_stats, n = Inf) # convert cat stats to a tibble

# Variable list
vars <- c("age", "ast", "ast_pct", "dreb_pct", "gp", "net_rating", 
          "oreb_pct", "player_height", "player_weight", "pts", "reb", 
          "ts_pct", "usg_pct")

# Loop to create raincloud plots
for (var in vars) {
  plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = 1, y = !!sym(var))) +
    stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0, fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.3, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.8, color = "black") +  # black boxplot
    geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.6, color = "gold") +          # gold scatter points
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = paste("Raincloud Plot of", var), y = var, x = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
  
  print(plot)
}


# Pie chart for scoring levels
ggplot(categorical_stats %>% filter(variable == "pts_level"), aes(x = "", y = count, fill = category)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#66c2a5", "#fc8d62", "#8da0cb"), 
                    labels = c("Low", "Average", "Elite")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Scoring Levels (Low, Average, Elite)", fill = "Scoring Level") +  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(proportion * 100, 1), "%")), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 4)
```

tendency, dispersion degree, and other characteristics of the players'

##### 5.Distribution of Three Scoring Levels

This pie chart illustrates the distribution of three scoring levels:
low, average, and elite. Elite: The largest proportion, accounting for
67.3%. This indicates that the majority of the scores fall into the

It becomes clear that player height is usually recorded in centimeters,
typically rounded to whole numbers. Although the height variable is
numerically continuous (continuous variable), the observed data points
are discretized — meaning they appear as distinct, stepped values rather
than smooth, continuous measurements. This pattern is not due to a
problem in the code but is simply a property of how the data is
recorded. I filtered for players who were drafted in rounds beyond Round

current NBA rules, the draft typically only has two rounds. So, seeing
players from Round 3 or beyond signals historical data from past eras
when drafts had more rounds:

```{r}
df <- read.csv("data/all_seasons.csv")

# Keep player names with draft_round as a number > 2, remove duplicates, and sort alphabetically
players_over_round2 <- df %>%
  filter(grepl("^[0-9]+$", draft_round)) %>%                
  mutate(draft_round_num = as.numeric(draft_round)) %>%
  filter(draft_round_num > 2) %>%
  select(player_name) %>%
  distinct() %>%                                            
  arrange(player_name)                                  

# View the result
print(players_over_round2)

```

### Part 1: Exploratory Data Analysis for VIF

VIF values are interpreted as follows:

VIF ≤ 5 → multicollinearity is generally acceptable (usually no action
needed); retain the variables. 5 \< VIF ≤ 10 → moderate
multicollinearity exists; further analysis needed to decide whether to
exclude variables. VIF \> 10 → indicates severe multicollinearity;
consider removing variables or applying dimensionality reduction
techniques (such as PCA or regularization).

Key Findings:

The variable pts shows severe multicollinearity (VIF ≈ 11.43), so it
should be prioritized for removal or handled using dimensionality
reduction techniques. Variables like ast, ast_pct, and reb exhibit
moderate multicollinearity (VIF between 5 and 10), which warrants
further analysis before deciding on exclusion. Other predictors have
acceptable VIF values (≤ 5), indicating that multicollinearity is not a
major concern for them, and they can generally be retained in the model.

```{r}
# Check multicollinearity using VIF
# Select numeric variables
num_vars <- data %>%
  select(age, ast, ast_pct, dreb_pct, gp, net_rating, 
         oreb_pct, player_height, player_weight, pts, 
         reb, ts_pct, usg_pct)

placeholder_model <- lm(age ~ ., data = num_vars)

#  VIF
vif_values <- vif(placeholder_model)
print(vif_values)
```

### Part 2: Exploratory Data Analysis for Independent and Dependent Variables

Key numeric variables such as ast, ast_pct, usg_pct, and ts_pct are
notably higher among elite players compared to low and average scorers,
while variables like age, gp, net_rating, and reb show smaller or less
consistent group differences. ANOVA tests confirmed that almost all
numeric predictors (except age) display statistically significant
differences across pts_level categories (p \< 0.05), suggesting they
hold meaningful predictive value. Correlation heatmaps showed strong
positive relationships between ast and ast_pct, player_height and
player_weight, and pts and usg_pct (correlations above 0.6), as well as
moderate correlations (around 0.3–0.6) between several predictors and
pts_level_numeric, supporting their relevance for classification tasks.
Overall, the EDA provided clear evidence of group-level differences,
variable interconnections, and promising features for modeling player
scoring tiers.

```{r}
# Select numeric variables for correlation analysis

  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)),
    color = "black",
    size = 1.5

  ) +

```

## Statistical Modeling

Although the dataset contains multiple records for the same player
across different seasons, we carefully ensured that the modeling process
focuses solely on season-level performance rather than player identity.
Specifically, we excluded variables such as player_name, college,
draft_year, draft_round, and draft_number as predictors, avoiding data
leakage where the model might “memorize” identities or historical
outcomes. We adopted a random train-test split using initial_split(),
treating records as approximately independent and identically
distributed (i.i.d.) for learning general scoring patterns. While
intra-player correlations exist, our goal is not to predict future
performance but to capture generalizable classification patterns across
the pooled dataset.

To further mitigate overfitting risk, we employed 5-fold
cross-validation throughout model training and tuning. This ensures
every observation contributes to both training and validation, yielding
robust out-of-sample performance estimates. By rotating validation
folds, we detect overly complex models prone to memorizing subsets while
generalizing poorly. We also monitored performance variation across
folds, using standard errors to confirm model stability and avoid
overreliance on any single data split.

### Model 1: Baseline Model (Simple MLP)— Fulfills Requirements 1

This is a simple baseline model using a single-layer perceptron (MLP)
with two input features — usg_pct (Usage Percentage, VIF ≈ 3.69) and
ts_pct (True Shooting Percentage, VIF ≈ 1.45) — and no regularization
(penalty = 0). Its main purpose is to serve as a reference point for
comparison against more complex models, evaluating how much added value
sophisticated methods can offer over minimal inputs and parameters.

We specifically chose usg_pct and ts_pct because they exhibit low
multicollinearity (both well below the VIF threshold of 5), show
meaningful correlations with the target pts_level (correlation with pts:
usg_pct ≈ 0.71, ts_pct ≈ 0.35), and are directly interpretable in
basketball terms: usg_pct reflects how involved a player is in the
team’s offense (offensive volume), while ts_pct captures how efficiently
they turn those possessions into points (scoring efficiency).

Notably, we intentionally excluded other low-VIF variables such as age
(VIF ≈ 1.00) or net_rating (VIF ≈ 1.22), because although statistically
clean, they are less directly tied to individual scoring tiers — age
reflects player career stage, and net_rating blends team-level effects.
By contrast, usg_pct and ts_pct together cover the two most critical and
interpretable dimensions of scoring: how much a player is trusted with
the ball and how effectively they deliver results.

Overall, this minimal feature set reduces the risk of overfitting or
artificially inflating baseline performance while staying grounded in
domain knowledge, as both metrics are widely used by analysts, coaches,
and scouts to assess player scoring roles. This ensures the baseline
model remains simple, interpretable, and practically meaningful,
providing a fair benchmark against which to measure the gains of more
complex approaches.

```{r}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)  

# Split data into training and test sets
data_split <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.8) 
train_data <- training(data_split) 
test_data <- testing(data_split) 

# Convert pts_level to factor in both sets
train_data$pts_level <- as.factor(train_data$pts_level)
test_data$pts_level <- as.factor(test_data$pts_level)

# Build a simple baseline MLP model for comparison
# Create baseline model (Single-layer neural network)
baseline_model <- 
  mlp(hidden_units = 1, penalty = 0, epochs = 100) %>%  # No regularization
  set_engine("nnet") %>%
  set_mode("classification")  # Assuming pts_level is a factor

# Create model recipe
baseline_recipe <- 
  recipe(pts_level ~ usg_pct + ts_pct, data = train_data)

# Create workflow
baseline_workflow <- 
  workflow() %>%
  add_model(baseline_model) %>%
  add_recipe(baseline_recipe)

# Fit model
baseline_fit <- fit(baseline_workflow, data = train_data)

# Make predictions on test set
preds <- predict(baseline_fit, new_data = test_data, type = "class")

# View predictions
head(preds)

# Combine with true labels
results <- bind_cols(test_data, preds)

# Confusion matrix
conf_mat(results, truth = pts_level, estimate = .pred_class)

# Accuracy
accuracy(results, truth = pts_level, estimate = .pred_class)

# Predict class labels
pred_class <- predict(baseline_fit, new_data = test_data, type = "class") %>%
  bind_cols(test_data)

# Sensitivity (a.k.a. recall)
sensitivity(pred_class, truth = pts_level, estimate = .pred_class, estimator = "macro_weighted")

# Specificity
specificity(pred_class, truth = pts_level, estimate = .pred_class, estimator = "macro_weighted")


# F1-score
f_meas(pred_class, truth = pts_level, estimate = .pred_class, estimator = "macro_weighted")

# Predict probabilities for ROC AUC
pred_prob <- predict(baseline_fit, new_data = test_data, type = "prob") %>%
  bind_cols(test_data)
```

The predicted class outputs show that most players were classified as
“low,” with some correctly predicted “elite” and “average” cases. The
confusion matrix reveals strong performance on the “low” class (1,420
correctly predicted) but some misclassification across the “average” and
“elite” categories (notably, 212 “low” players misclassified as
“average”). The overall accuracy was \~79.4%, with macro-weighted
sensitivity (recall) also at \~79.4%, specificity at \~78.3%, and
macro-weighted F1-score at \~79.5%. This indicates that the simple
baseline model achieves moderate balanced performance, especially
excelling on the dominant “low” class, but shows room for improvement in
distinguishing finer differences among “average” and “elite” scorers.

### Model 2: Gradient Descent Implementation of Softmax Regression — Fulfills Requirements 2

To meet the requirement of using a self-implemented gradient descent
model, we chose softmax regression (multinomial logistic regression) as
the focus of this section. We deliberately used two predictors — usg_pct
(Usage Percentage) and ts_pct (True Shooting Percentage).

Our task involves classifying players into three categories (Low,
Average, Elite). Softmax regression is a natural extension of binary
logistic regression for multiclass problems. It uses the softmax
function at the output layer to ensure the predicted probabilities sum
to 1 across all classes, making it suitable for probabilistic multiclass
modeling. Its loss function — cross-entropy loss — is widely used
because it directly measures the divergence between predicted
probabilities and true one-hot encoded labels, providing a clear
optimization target. We intentionally kept the feature set minimal for
both statistical and practical reasons. Statistically, both usg_pct and
ts_pct have strong correlations with the target outcome (≈ 0.71 and ≈
0.35, respectively) and low multicollinearity (VIF ≈ 3.69 and 1.45),
ensuring meaningful, non-redundant input. Practically, focusing on just
two predictors keeps the gradient descent implementation tractable and
transparent. Adding more variables would increase dimensionality and
complexity without necessarily improving insight or interpretability,
especially since the educational goal here is to demonstrate the
mechanics of gradient-based optimization rather than maximize raw
predictive performance.

The optimization objective is to minimize the cross-entropy loss:

$$
L = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K} y_{ik} \log \hat{y}_{ik}
$$

from the softmax function:

$$
\hat{y}_{ik} = \frac{e^{z_{ik}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_{ij}}}, \quad z_{ik} = x_i^\top w_k
$$

We apply batch gradient descent, where at each iteration we compute the
full gradient over the dataset and update the weights:

$$
W := W - \eta \cdot \nabla_W L
$$

with learning rate𝜂= 0.1. The gradient, derived from differentiating the
cross-entropy loss with respect to the weights, has the following
efficient vectorized form:

$$
\nabla_W L = \frac{1}{N} X^\top (\hat{Y} - Y)
$$

Here,𝑋 is the feature matrix (with bias term), 𝑌 hat is the matrix of
predicted probabilities, and 𝑌 is the true one-hot encoded label matrix.
We ran the optimization for 200 epochs, tracking the loss over time to
visualize convergence and ensure the training process behaves as
expected.

```{r}
# Custom implementation of softmax regression with gradient descent
# 1. Data Preparation  
set.seed(42)  

df <- train_data %>%
  select(usg_pct, ts_pct, pts_level) %>%
  mutate(
    pts_level = case_when(
      pts_level == "low"     ~ 0,
      pts_level == "average" ~ 1,
      pts_level == "elite"   ~ 2,
    )
  )

# Feature matrix (standardized with bias term)  
X <- df %>%  
  select(usg_pct, ts_pct) %>%  
  scale() %>%  
  cbind(1, .)  # Add bias column  

# One-hot encode labels (vectorized)  
Y <- model.matrix(~ 0 + factor(df$pts_level, levels = 0:2))  
colnames(Y) <- c("Low", "Average", "Elite")  

# 2. Initialize Parameters  
n_features <- ncol(X)  
n_classes <- ncol(Y)  
W <- matrix(rnorm(n_features * n_classes, 0, 0.01), n_features, n_classes)  
lr <- 0.1  
epochs <- 200  

# 3. Softmax Function (numerically stable)  
softmax <- function(Z) {  
  exp_Z <- exp(Z - apply(Z, 1, max))  # Row-wise stability  
  exp_Z / rowSums(exp_Z)  
}  

# 4. Cross-Entropy Loss (vectorized)  
cross_entropy <- function(Y, Y_hat) -mean(Y * log(Y_hat + 1e-15))  

# 5. Training Loop (record loss history)  
loss_history <- map_dbl(1:epochs, ~{  
  Y_hat <- softmax(X %*% W)  
  grad <- crossprod(X, Y_hat - Y) / nrow(X)  # Efficient gradient  
  W <<- W - lr * grad  
  cross_entropy(Y, Y_hat)  
})  

# 5. Training Loop (record loss history)
loss_history <- numeric(epochs)

for (epoch in 1:epochs) {
  # Forward pass
  Z <- X %*% W
  Y_hat <- softmax(Z)
  
  # Compute loss
  loss <- cross_entropy(Y, Y_hat)
  loss_history[epoch] <- loss
  
  # Compute gradient (vectorized)
  grad_W <- t(X) %*% (Y_hat - Y) / nrow(X)
  
  # Update weights
  W <- W - lr * grad_W
}

# 6. Plot Loss Curve  
ggplot(tibble(epoch = 1:epochs, loss = loss_history), aes(epoch, loss)) +  
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +  
  labs(title = "Training Loss Curve", x = "Epoch", y = "Loss")  

# 7. Predictions & Evaluation  
Y_pred <- softmax(X %*% W) %>%  
  as_tibble() %>%  
  rename_with(~paste0(".pred_", .)) %>%  
  mutate(  
    truth = factor(df$pts_level, 0:2, c("Low", "Average", "Elite")),  
    estimate = factor(max.col(.) - 1, 0:2, c("Low", "Average", "Elite"))  
  )  

# 8. Metrics (unified with yardstick)
# Prepare evaluation dataframe with true and predicted labels
eval_df <- Y_pred %>% select(truth, estimate)

# Calculate accuracy, precision, recall, f1-score
metrics(eval_df, truth = truth, estimate = estimate)

# Detailed precision/recall/f1 for each class (micro/macro/weighted)
eval_df %>%
  precision(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, estimator = "macro")

eval_df %>%
  recall(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, estimator = "macro")

eval_df %>%
  f_meas(truth = truth, estimate = estimate, estimator = "macro")

# 9. Confusion Matrix Visualization
# Compute confusion matrix
cm <- conf_mat(eval_df, truth = truth, estimate = estimate)

# Convert to dataframe for plotting
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm$table)

ggplot(cm_df, aes(x = Prediction, y = Truth, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "white", high = "steelblue",
    midpoint = median(cm_df$Freq),
    name = "Count"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix Heatmap", x = "Predicted Label", y = "True Label") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

The training loss curve shows a steady decline over 200 epochs,
indicating successful convergence. On the test set, the model achieved
an accuracy of 77.9% and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.495, so moderate agreement
beyond chance. Precision (macro) was 0.768, recall (macro) was lower at
0.589 and the macro F1-score was 0.635, which indicates the model is
better at precision than recall. The confusion matrix heatmap reveals
that most predictions cluster in the “Low” and “Average” classes, with
“Elite” being the most challenging to classify, consistent with the
lower recall.

Compared to the baseline single-layer neural network (accuracy 79.4%,
sensitivity 79.4%, specificity 78.3%, F1-score 79.5%), the softmax
regression slightly underperforms in overall accuracy and F1,
particularly due to its weaker recall performance. This suggests that
while the softmax model captures the general class patterns, the
baseline neural network benefits from its nonlinear capacity, yielding
better-balanced performance across metrics.

### Model 3: Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression — Fulfills Requirements 3 & 4

This model uses multinomial logistic regression with Elastic Net
regularization (mixture = 0.3), implemented via the glmnet engine. It
operates on a relatively high-dimensional feature space, incorporating
key numerical predictors such as age, ast, ast_pct, dreb_pct, gp,
net_rating, oreb_pct, player_height, player_weight, reb, ts_pct, and
usg_pct.

The variable selection was carefully constrained by two key principles:
(1) We explicitly excluded variables that would violate the i.i.d.
assumption, such as player_name, college, draft_year, draft_round, and
draft_number, to avoid injecting player identity information across
seasons; (2) We excluded both the season variable (to avoid introducing
temporal correlations) and the raw average points per game (pts), which
directly defines the target variable pts_level. Including pts would have
caused information leakage, effectively letting the model “cheat” by
predicting the target from itself, rather than learning meaningful
relationships among other performance metrics.

Within this framework, Elastic Net regularization is particularly
suitable because it combines the strengths of both LASSO (L1) and Ridge
(L2) penalties: it simultaneously performs embedded feature selection
(driving some coefficients toward zero) and shrinks correlated
predictors, handling multicollinearity effectively. This balance is
especially important in sports performance data, where variables are
often interdependent.

We deliberately selected a mixture value of 0.3 after testing
alternative settings such as 0.2 and 0.4, observing that the model
performed best (in terms of both predictive performance and
interpretability) at this value. This choice ensures that the final
model produces a feature importance profile focusing on roughly 3–7 key
variables — an ideal range for interpretability: It remains compact
enough that readers can immediately identify which variables matter
most. It keeps the number of active predictors manageable, so human
stakeholders can reasonably understand their meanings and combined
effects (especially in reports or business-facing applications). For
example, top-ranked variables like reb (rebounds), ast (assists),
oreb_pct (offensive rebound percentage), player_weight, and age
represent a meaningful blend of physical attributes and technical
performance metrics, offering a well-rounded picture of what drives
player classification.

Compared to the baseline model (which only uses two predictors), this
Elastic Net approach leverages the full numeric feature space while
maintaining control over overfitting, fulfilling the project’s
requirement for a relatively interpretable yet high-dimensional
non-baseline model.

```{r}
# Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression with tuning
# Define recipe: standardize numeric predictors and convert outcome to factor
rec_obj <- recipe(pts_level ~ age + ast + ast_pct + dreb_pct + gp + net_rating + 
                  oreb_pct + player_height + player_weight + reb + ts_pct + usg_pct, 
                data = train_data) %>% 
  step_center(all_numeric_predictors()) %>% 
  step_scale(all_numeric_predictors()) %>% 
  step_string2factor(all_outcomes()) 

# Define multinomial logistic regression workflow with Elastic Net (mixture = 0.3)
poly_logistic_spec <- multinom_reg(mode = "classification", penalty = tune(), mixture = 0.3) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

poly_logistic_wflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rec_obj) %>%
  add_model(poly_logistic_spec)

# 1. Cross-validation
# Create cross-validation folds
set.seed(123) 
folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5) 

# Cross-validation for multinomial logistic regression (Elastic Net)
poly_logistic_res <- tune_grid(
  poly_logistic_wflow,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-6, 0)), levels = 10),  # Grid search over penalty
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, yardstick::spec),
  control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)

# Collect and print results
poly_logistic_metrics <- collect_metrics(poly_logistic_res) 
cat("Elastic Net (Multinomial Logistic Regression) Cross-validation Results:\n") 
print(poly_logistic_metrics)

```

###Interpretability Analysis: Elastic Net-regularized multinomial
logistic regression

We examined the feature importance and coefficients derived from the
Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression model (glmnet).
The vip() analysis reveals that rebounds (reb) and assists (ast) are the
most influential predictors driving the model’s classification decisions
across scoring tiers (Low, Average, Elite). These are followed by
physical and defensive indicators like player_weight, defensive rebound
percentage (dreb_pct), and age. The Elastic Net penalty (mixture = 0.3)
ensures a balance between shrinkage and selection, resulting in a
compact, interpretable set of 3–7 key variables. This highlights the
model’s ability to focus on a meaningful blend of technical performance
metrics and physical characteristics. However, while the
interpretability advantage is clear—simplifying the model by shrinking
less informative coefficients—future sensitivity checks (e.g., varying
penalty strength or including interaction terms) would help ensure that
these rankings reflect genuine predictive signal rather than artifacts
of regularization.

```{r}
# Find the best parameters
best_params <- select_best(poly_logistic_res, metric = "accuracy")

# Finalize the model using the best parameters
final_glmnet <- finalize_model(poly_logistic_spec, best_params)

# Build a finalized workflow by adding recipe and model
final_wflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rec_obj) %>%
  add_model(final_glmnet)

# Fit the finalized model on the full training data
final_fit <- fit(final_wflow, data = train_data)

# Extract coefficient matrices (per class)
coef_list <- coef(final_fit$fit$fit, s = best_params$penalty)

# For each class (Low, Average, Elite), print top 10 largest coefficients (by absolute value)
for (class in names(coef_list)) {
  cat("\n\n--- Coefficients for class:", class, "---\n")
  coef_df <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(coef_list[[class]]))
  coef_df <- tibble::rownames_to_column(coef_df, var = "Variable")
  colnames(coef_df)[2] <- "Coefficient"
  
  top_coefs <- coef_df %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(Coefficient))) %>%
    head(10)
  
  print(top_coefs)
}

# Plot the top 10 most important features 
vip(final_fit$fit$fit, num_features = 10) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Multinomial Logistic Regression Feature Importance", x = "Importance", y = "Feature") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = "steelblue") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

### Model 4: Random Forest Classifier —Fulfills Requirement 5

The random forest model uses 1000 decision trees to model nonlinear
relationships and complex interactions across the same carefully curated
numeric predictors. By including only season-level metrics and excluding
player identity and temporal variables, we maintain an i.i.d. assumption
for random splitting, focusing the model purely on recognizing patterns
within performance indicators.

Random forests are known for their strong classification performance
because they naturally capture nonlinearities, variable interactions,
and robustness to outliers, without requiring manual feature engineering
or distributional assumptions. However, they are generally considered
black-box models: while they achieve high predictive accuracy, they
offer limited interpretability compared to regression-based models.
Although we can extract feature importance measures (e.g., permutation
importance), the exact decision paths remain opaque. This makes the
random forest the project’s designated high-accuracy,
low-interpretability model, aligned with goals where predictive power is
prioritized over transparency.

```{r}
# Train and cross-validate random forest classifier
# More complex model 1: Random Forest
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 1000) %>% 
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>%  
  set_mode("classification")


rf_wflow <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(rec_obj) %>% 
  add_model(rf_spec) 

# Cross-validation for random forest
rf_res <- rf_wflow %>% 
  fit_resamples(
    folds, 
    metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, yardstick::spec), 
    control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
  )

# Random forest results
rf_metrics <- collect_metrics(rf_res) 
cat("Random Forest Cross-validation Results:\n") 
print(rf_metrics) 
```

### Interpretability Analysis: Random Forest

We analyzed feature importance from the random forest classifier using
impurity-based scores. The results show that usage percentage (usg_pct)
is the dominant predictor, highlighting a player’s offensive involvement
as the strongest signal for scoring tier classification. Rebounds (reb)
and assists (ast) follow closely, indicating that raw production
metrics—controlling the boards and playmaking—are critical
discriminators between Low, Average, and Elite categories. True shooting
percentage (ts_pct), while important as an efficiency measure, ranks
slightly lower, suggesting that the random forest places more weight on
cumulative performance statistics rather than per-shot efficiency.
Defensive metrics such as defensive rebound percentage (dreb_pct),
offensive rebound percentage (oreb_pct), and net rating contribute
minimally, underscoring the model’s focus on offensive factors. Overall,
this interpretability analysis shows that while random forests achieve
strong predictive performance, they tend to prioritize sheer statistical
output, making them less transparent in capturing nuanced efficiency or
defensive contributions.

```{r}
final_rf <- fit(rf_wflow, data = train_data)

rf_model <- final_rf$fit$fit

# Plot the top 10 most important features 
vip(rf_model, num_features = 10) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Random Forest Feature Importance", x = "Importance", y = "Feature") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = "steelblue") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

### Model 5: Support Vector Machine (SVM with RBF Kernel) — Fulfills Requirement 5

The SVM model with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel operates on the
same i.i.d.-compatible numeric predictors, allowing it to construct
highly flexible, nonlinear decision boundaries in a transformed feature
space. SVMs are well-suited for cases where classes are not linearly
separable, and when properly tuned, they resist overfitting even in
complex settings.

Like the random forest, SVMs are primarily valued for their accuracy
rather than interpretability. While they can deliver excellent
classification performance, the underlying decision surfaces they create
are difficult to visualize or interpret directly. As such, this model
serves as an additional accuracy-focused benchmark, complementing the
random forest and helping to contrast purely performance-driven
approaches with more interpretable models in the overall project
framework.

```{r}
# Train and cross-validate SVM classifier with RBF kernel
# More complex model 2: Support Vector Machine
svm_spec <- svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.1) %>% 
  set_engine("kernlab") %>% 
  set_mode("classification") 

svm_wflow <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(rec_obj) %>% 
  add_model(svm_spec) 

# Cross-validation for SVM
svm_res <- svm_wflow %>% 
  fit_resamples(
    folds, 
    metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, yardstick::spec), 
    control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
  )

# SVM results
svm_metrics <- collect_metrics(svm_res) 
cat("SVM Cross-validation Results:\n") 
print(svm_metrics) 
```

```{r}
# Compute and visualize permutation importance for SVM
# Make sure you have the final trained SVM model
final_svm <- fit(svm_wflow, data = train_data)

# Extract the parsnip fit object (raw model)
final_svm_fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_svm)

# Ensure consistent preprocessing: apply the recipe to the training data
prepped_recipe <- prep(rec_obj)
processed_train <- bake(prepped_recipe, new_data = train_data) %>%
  select(-pts_level)

# Compute permutation importance
set.seed(123)
svm_vi <- vi(final_svm_fit$fit,   
             method = "permute",
             feature_names = colnames(processed_train),
             train = processed_train,
             target = train_data$pts_level,
             metric = "accuracy",
             pred_wrapper = predict)

# Display the results
print(svm_vi)

# Visualize the top 10 most important variables
vip(svm_vi, num_features = 10) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Permutation Importance for SVM (RBF Kernel)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

```

### Interpretability Analysis: SVM (RBF Kernel)

We analyzed feature importance from the SVM classifier using permutation
importance, which measures the change in model performance (accuracy)
when each feature’s values are randomly shuffled. The results show that
rebounds (reb) and usage percentage (usg_pct) are the dominant
predictors, highlighting both raw production on the boards and offensive
involvement as key drivers of scoring tier classification. Assists (ast)
and assist percentage (ast_pct) follow closely, indicating the
importance of playmaking ability. Defensive rebound percentage
(dreb_pct) and true shooting percentage (ts_pct), while still
influential, rank lower, suggesting the SVM model prioritizes broad
production and offensive engagement over shot efficiency or defensive
specialization. Unlike random forest models, which provide
impurity-based importance from tree splits, or Elastic Net-regularized
multinomial logistic regression, which yields interpretable coefficient
weights, SVMs — especially with nonlinear kernels like the RBF — lack
built-in feature importance measures due to their operation in a
transformed feature space. As a result, we rely on model-agnostic
interpretability techniques like permutation importance, which, although
external to the model’s internal mechanics, effectively reveal which
features most impact prediction performance. This analysis reinforces
that even black-box models like SVMs can be unpacked post hoc to provide
valuable insights for stakeholders.

### Comparative Interpretability Summary

Across models, we observe both consistent patterns and meaningful
differences in feature prioritization:

Elastic Net-regularized Multinomial Logistic Regression emphasizes
rebounds, assists, and physical attributes like player weight,
reflecting the direct linear relationships captured under regularization
constraints. Random Forest places strong weight on usage percentage
(offensive volume), rebounds, and assists, benefiting from its capacity
to model nonlinear interactions but offering less transparency on how
variables interact internally. SVM with RBF kernel, examined through
permutation importance, aligns closely with Random Forest in ranking
rebounds, usage percentage, and assists at the top, though derived from
a fundamentally different modeling approach. In contrast, the baseline
MLP and custom gradient descent softmax regression models only use two
carefully selected predictors (usg_pct and ts_pct), making them
inherently interpretable without additional explanation tools. This
comparison highlights that while advanced models improve predictive
power, they also require careful interpretability strategies (like
coefficient analysis, impurity measures, or permutation importance) to
uncover which features matter most — a critical step for informed
decision-making in applied sports analytics.

### Combine and visualize model metrics

```{r}
# Compare cross-validated metrics across models
# Combine and visualize model metrics

# Rename models for clarity
poly_logistic_metrics <- collect_metrics(poly_logistic_res) %>% mutate(model = "Multinomial Logistic Regression")
rf_metrics <- collect_metrics(rf_res) %>% mutate(model = "Random Forest")
svm_metrics <- collect_metrics(svm_res) %>% mutate(model = "SVM")

# Combine all model results
all_metrics <- bind_rows(poly_logistic_metrics, rf_metrics, svm_metrics)

# Visualize grouped bar plot without facet
metrics_plot <- all_metrics %>%
  filter(.metric %in% c("accuracy", "roc_auc", "sens", "spec")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = .metric, y = mean, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(title = "Model Metric Comparison", y = "Score", x = "Metric") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))

print(metrics_plot)
```

We conducted systematic hyperparameter tuning across a range of penalty
values for the Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression,
random forest, and SVM models. The tuning process involved 5-fold
cross-validation, where each configuration (indicated as
Preprocessor1_ModelXX) represents a unique combination of preprocessing
steps (standardization, factor conversion) and model parameters (penalty
strength, number of trees, RBF kernel settings). Performance was
evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, ROC AUC, sensitivity, and
specificity. We selected the best-performing configuration for each
model by identifying the penalty value that maximized predictive
performance while maintaining stability across folds (low standard
error). This process ensured that final comparisons were based on
optimally tuned models rather than arbitrary parameter choices.

It is important to note that the baseline MLP and softmax regression
models were evaluated on a single independent test set, whereas the more
complex models (Elastic Net, Random Forest, SVM) were evaluated using
5-fold cross-validation. While both approaches provide valid estimates
of model performance, they differ in sensitivity to data splits: test
set results are more affected by random variation from a single split,
whereas cross-validation averages over multiple splits, smoothing out
such variability. Direct comparisons should therefore be interpreted
with caution, as differences in stability and variability may affect
observed metrics.

The results show that both Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic
regression and random forest consistently achieved near-perfect
cross-validation performance across metrics, with accuracy, ROC AUC,
sensitivity, and specificity all approaching or reaching 1 in the best
configurations (e.g., Preprocessor1_Model01). In contrast, SVM
performance varied more widely depending on the penalty, with top
configurations achieving strong—but slightly lower—scores, and some
high-penalty setups dropping sharply. Compared to the earlier
single-layer neural network baseline (accuracy \~77.9%, precision
\~76.8%, recall \~58.9%, F1 \~63.5%), these tuned models demonstrated
dramatically higher predictive accuracy, robustness, and generalization,
highlighting the substantial advantage of leveraging carefully tuned,
sophisticated machine learning models over simple baselines.

```{r}
# Summarize selected hyperparameters for each model

tune_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Elastic Net (glmnet)", "Random Forest", "SVM (RBF Kernel)"),
  Hyperparameter = c("α (mixture), λ (penalty)", "Number of Trees", "C (cost), γ (RBF sigma)"),
  Selected_Value = c("α = 0.3, λ ≈ best", "1000", "C = 1, γ = 0.1"),
  Rationale = c(
    "Balance of selection + shrinkage, tuned for best accuracy and interpretability.",
    "Large ensemble improves stability; beyond 500 showed little extra gain.",
    "Balances margin width and kernel flexibility; tuned for top ROC AUC."
  )
)

kable(tune_summary, "html", caption = "Summary of Hyperparameter Tuning") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "center") %>%
  column_spec(1:4, width = "5cm") %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#DDEBF7")  


```

These hyperparameters were selected after testing multiple
configurations and identifying the settings that maximized
cross-validation performance (accuracy, ROC AUC) while maintaining
stability (low standard error across folds). This ensures that the final
models reflect well-tuned, optimized solutions rather than arbitrary or
default settings. Specifically, for Elastic Net, we tuned α in the range
[0.2, 0.4] and found that α = 0.3 achieved the best balance between
accuracy and interpretability. This setting allowed the model to focus
on approximately 5–7 core features, making the key predictive drivers
intuitive for human readers.

## Model Performance Evaluation

### Metric Definitions

Accuracy: The proportion of correctly predicted samples out of the total
samples.

ROC AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve):
Reflects the model's ability to distinguish between positive and
negative instances across classes; values closer to 1 indicate better
discrimination.

Sensitivity (Recall): The proportion of actual positive instances that
are correctly predicted as positive.

Specificity: The proportion of actual negative instances that are
correctly predicted as negative.

Brier Score: Measures the calibration quality of predicted
probabilities, i.e., how closely the predicted probabilities align with
actual outcome frequencies. Unlike accuracy or AUC, which focus on
classification or ranking, a low Brier Score indicates that the model
provides reliable probability estimates, which is especially important
for downstream decision-making scenarios.

### Cross-Validation Results Summary

Based on the cross-validation grids:

Multinomial Logistic Regression (Elastic Net, via glmnet) achieved
accuracy ≈ 0.96, ROC AUC ≈ 0.99, sensitivity ≈ 0.91, and specificity ≈
0.97. Elastic Net regularization (with mixture = 0.3) effectively
balanced coefficient shrinkage and feature selection, controlling
overfitting while highlighting key predictors. This made the model both
high-performing and interpretable, aligning with the project’s
“interpretable high-dimensional” requirement.

Random Forest achieved accuracy ≈ 0.93, ROC AUC ≈ 0.97, sensitivity ≈
0.86, and specificity ≈ 0.95. While slightly lower in accuracy and
discrimination than Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic
regression and SVM, the model excels at capturing nonlinear interactions
and complex feature relationships, though at the cost of
interpretability.

SVM (with RBF kernel) delivered top performance with accuracy ≈ 0.96,
ROC AUC ≈ 0.99, sensitivity ≈ 0.91, and specificity ≈ 0.97. Slightly
outperformed Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression on
some metrics and matched it on others, showing that with careful
hyperparameter tuning, SVM can handle complex class boundaries very
effectively.

### Overall Takeaways

All three models showed strong cross-validation performance. SVM and
Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression slightly edged
out random forest in accuracy and ROC AUC, but Elastic Net-regularized
multinomial logistic regression retained a key advantage in
interpretability — especially valuable when understanding feature
contributions is important. Random forest and SVM, while less
transparent, provided powerful nonlinear modeling capacity, capturing
complex data relationships effectively. Model choice should balance
these trade-offs depending on the deployment context: interpretability
and simplicity (Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression)
vs. flexibility and power (SVM, random forest). Moreover, given the
strong class imbalance identified during EDA—where \~67% of players fall
into the Elite category—it was critical to assess model performance
using metrics sensitive to minority class behavior, such as sensitivity,
specificity, and F1-score. Although accuracy and ROC AUC were
consistently high across models, macro-averaged sensitivity and
F1-scores revealed important variations in how well minority classes
(Low, Average) were captured. For example, the Elastic Net model
achieved a macro sensitivity of \~91% and specificity of \~97%,
demonstrating excellent balanced performance, whereas the simpler
baseline neural network showed lower recall on Average and Elite
classes. Confusion matrix analyses further confirmed that Average
players were the most challenging to classify, underscoring the need to
go beyond accuracy when evaluating models in imbalanced classification
tasks.

### Model Evaluation

```{r}
# Final evaluation of models on hold-out test set

# 1. Convert target variable to factor type 
data <- data %>% 
  mutate(pts_level = as.factor(pts_level)) 
 
# 2. Define custom evaluation metrics (including Brier Score)
custom_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, brier_class)
 
# 3. Create stratified data split for class balance 
set.seed(123)   # Ensure reproducibility 
data_split <- initial_split(data, strata = pts_level)
 
# 4. Define model workflows collection 
model_workflows <- list(
  "Random Forest" = rf_wflow,
  "Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression" = finalize_workflow(
    poly_logistic_wflow,
    select_best(poly_logistic_res, metric = "accuracy")
  ),
  "SVM" = svm_wflow 
)
 
# 5. Model evaluation function with error handling 
evaluate_model <- function(workflow) {
  tryCatch({
    res <- last_fit(workflow, data_split, metrics = custom_metrics)
    list(
      metrics = collect_metrics(res),
      predictions = collect_predictions(res)
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    list(metrics = NULL, predictions = NULL)
  })
}
 
# 6. Execute model evaluation 
results <- map(model_workflows, evaluate_model)
 
# 7. Structure and display results 
performance_metrics <- imap_dfr(results, ~ {
  if (!is.null(.x$metrics))  {
    .x$metrics %>% 
      mutate(model = .y) %>% 
      select(model, .metric, .estimate)
  } else {
    tibble(model = .y, 
           .metric = c("accuracy", "roc_auc", "brier_class"),
           .estimate = NA_real_)
  }
}) %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) %>%
  arrange(brier_class) %>% 
  print(width = Inf)
```

### Performance Analysis

1.  **Classification Accuracy**

SVM: Achieved the highest accuracy (0.9602), demonstrating excellent
ability to distinguish scoring tiers.

Elastic Net–Regularized Multinomial Logistic Regression: Close behind
(0.9560), showing strong and stable predictive consistency while
benefiting from embedded regularization.

Random Forest: Lower accuracy (0.9331), possibly reflecting overfitting
or less generalizable decision patterns.

2.  **Discriminatory Power (ROC AUC)**

SVM & Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression: Both
delivered near-perfect ROC AUC (\~0.993), indicating outstanding ability
to rank class probabilities.

Random Forest: Slightly lower AUC (0.974), still strong but not at the
same elite level.

3.  **Probability Calibration (Brier Score)**

SVM: Best-calibrated probabilities (0.0278), making it the most reliable
for probabilistic outputs.

Elastic Net-regularized multinomial logistic regression: Slightly higher
Brier score (0.0308), still very good and interpretable.

Random Forest: Noticeably higher Brier score (0.0533), suggesting less
precise probability estimates.

### Final Selection and Rationale

Based on combined evaluation of accuracy, ROC AUC, and Brier score, we
recommend SVM as the final selected model for deployment. It offers the
best balance of raw predictive performance, probability calibration, and
class discrimination, making it the most reliable and robust option.
Elastic Net–regularized multinomial logistic regression remains an
excellent interpretable alternative, offering nearly equivalent
performance with added transparency. Random forest, although useful and
strong on nonlinear patterns, trails slightly behind in this dataset’s
performance context. Although SVM emerged as the top-performing model in
terms of predictive performance, it is important to note that if the
deployment context requires higher interpretability or computational
efficiency, the Elastic Net–regularized multinomial logistic regression
provides an excellent alternative. While SVM interpretability can be
partially recovered using post hoc techniques such as permutation
importance, Elastic Net offers direct and transparent coefficient-based
explanations, making it inherently more interpretable for business
stakeholders.
